front: Benedict's test: method and positive result?
back: Equal volume of Benedict's, heat in a water bath; blue → green/yellow/orange/brick-red with reducing sugar.

front: Why does sucrose give a negative Benedict's result?
back: Its glycosidic bond joins the reducing groups of glucose and fructose; it must be hydrolysed first.

front: Steps of the non-reducing sugar test?
back: Benedict's negative; boil fresh sample with dilute HCl; cool; neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate; Benedict's again → brick-red.
Iodine in potassium iodide: orange-brown → blue-black.
Shake with ethanol, pour into water: milky-white emulsion.
Biuret reagent (NaOH + dilute CuSO₄), no heat: blue → lilac/purple; detects peptide bonds.

front: What is a semi-quantitative Benedict's test?
back: A standardised test compared with standards of known concentration (colours or time to first colour change) to estimate concentration.
A graph of a measured value (absorbance or % transmission) against known concentrations, used to read off an unknown.

front: Why use excess Benedict's in a quantitative test?
back: So copper(II) ions never run out; the result then depends only on the sugar concentration.
